questions.q: According to the Brønsted-Lowry theory, an acid is:
questions.solution:
A Brønsted-Lowry acid is a **proton donor**, a base a proton acceptor.

The Lewis definition is broader — an acid is an **electron pair acceptor** — which is why $\text{BF}_{3}$ counts as a Lewis acid despite having no proton to give.

questions.q: The pH of $0.01$ mol dm$^{-3}$ HCl is:
questions.solution:
HCl is a strong acid and fully dissociates, so $[\text{H}^{+}] = 0.01 = 10^{-2}$.

$\text{pH} = -\log 10^{-2} = \mathbf{2}$.

questions.q: A buffer solution is made from:
questions.solution:
A **weak acid and its conjugate base** — ethanoic acid with sodium ethanoate, for instance.

A reservoir of both species is needed: the acid mops up added alkali, the salt mops up added acid.
options: a strong acid and its salt
a weak acid and its conjugate base

questions.q: The standard hydrogen electrode is assigned a potential of:
questions.solution:
**Exactly zero**, by definition, at $298$ K, $100$ kPa and $1$ mol dm$^{-3}$ $\text{H}^{+}$.

Only differences in potential can be measured, so one electrode has to be chosen as the reference.

questions.q: A redox reaction is feasible under standard conditions when $E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}$ is:
questions.solution:
A **positive** cell potential means a negative $\Delta G$, so the reaction is thermodynamically feasible.

Feasible does not mean fast, though: a large positive $E^{\ominus}$ with a high activation energy may still give no observable reaction.

questions.q: Find the pH of $0.001$ mol dm$^{-3}$ nitric acid.
A solution has $\text{pOH} = 4$. Find its pH.
Find $E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}$ (in V) for a cell with electrode potentials $-0.76$ V and $+0.34$ V.
questions.solution:
$E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\ominus}_{\text{anode}} = 0.34 - (-0.76) = \mathbf{1.10}$ V.

The more positive electrode is always the cathode, where reduction occurs.

questions.q: A weak acid has $[\text{H}^{+}] = 10^{-4}$ mol dm$^{-3}$. Find its pH.
How many faradays are needed to deposit $1$ mol of aluminium from $\text{Al}^{3+}$?
questions.solution:
$\text{Al}^{3+} + 3e^{-} \to \text{Al}$ — $\mathbf{3}$ faradays per mole.

That triple charge is a large part of why aluminium extraction is so expensive in electricity.

questions.q: Distinguish between a strong and a weak acid, define $K_{a}$ and $\text{p}K_{a}$, and calculate the pH of $0.1$ mol dm$^{-3}$ ethanoic acid ($K_{a} = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$).
questions.solution:
**Strong acid** — fully dissociated in water. HCl, $\text{HNO}_{3}$, $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$.

**Weak acid** — only partly dissociated, with an equilibrium between the acid and its ions.

$\text{HA} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^{+} + \text{A}^{-}$

**Strength is not concentration.** A concentrated solution of a weak acid can have a lower pH than a dilute strong one — the two words describe different things entirely.

**The acid dissociation constant:**

$K_{a} = \dfrac{[\text{H}^{+}][\text{A}^{-}]}{[\text{HA}]}$, and $\text{p}K_{a} = -\log K_{a}$

A **larger $K_{a}$** (or smaller $\text{p}K_{a}$) means a stronger acid.

**The calculation.** Two approximations are standard:

1. $[\text{H}^{+}] = [\text{A}^{-}]$, since both come from the same dissociation.

2. $[\text{HA}]$ at equilibrium $\approx$ its initial value, since so little dissociates.

$K_{a} = \dfrac{[\text{H}^{+}]^{2}}{0.1}$

$[\text{H}^{+}]^{2} = 1.8 \times 10^{-6}$

$[\text{H}^{+}] = 1.34 \times 10^{-3}$

$\text{pH} = \mathbf{2.87}$

**Compare $0.1$ mol dm$^{-3}$ HCl at pH $1$** — the strong acid gives nearly a hundred times more hydrogen ions at the same concentration.

**Checking the approximation:** only $1.3\%$ of the ethanoic acid has dissociated, so assuming $[\text{HA}]$ unchanged was entirely safe. It would not be for a much stronger weak acid.

questions.q: Explain how a buffer solution resists a change in pH, and calculate the pH of a buffer containing $0.1$ mol dm$^{-3}$ ethanoic acid and $0.1$ mol dm$^{-3}$ sodium ethanoate ($K_{a} = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$).
questions.solution:
**What a buffer contains.** A reservoir of a weak acid **and** a reservoir of its conjugate base, with the equilibrium

$\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_{3}\text{COO}^{-} + \text{H}^{+}$

**On adding acid.** The extra $\text{H}^{+}$ is removed by the large reserve of ethanoate ions:

$\text{CH}_{3}\text{COO}^{-} + \text{H}^{+} \to \text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH}$

**On adding alkali.** The $\text{OH}^{-}$ is removed by the large reserve of undissociated acid:

$\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH} + \text{OH}^{-} \to \text{CH}_{3}\text{COO}^{-} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

In both cases the **ratio** $\dfrac{[\text{HA}]}{[\text{A}^{-}]}$ changes only slightly, so the pH barely moves.

**The calculation.** Rearranging $K_{a}$:

$[\text{H}^{+}] = K_{a}\dfrac{[\text{HA}]}{[\text{A}^{-}]} = 1.8 \times 10^{-5} \times 1 = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$

$\text{pH} = \mathbf{4.74}$

**When acid and salt are equal, $\text{pH} = \text{p}K_{a}$** — and a buffer works best at that point, where it has equal capacity in both directions.

**Choosing a buffer** therefore means choosing an acid whose $\text{p}K_{a}$ is near the pH wanted.

**Where buffers matter.** Blood is buffered by $\text{H}_{2}\text{CO}_{3}/\text{HCO}_{3}^{-}$ at pH $7.4$; a drift of more than about $0.4$ either way is fatal. Shampoos, fermentation vats and biochemical assays are all buffered for the same reason.

**A buffer has a finite capacity:** add enough acid to exhaust the ethanoate reserve and the pH collapses.

questions.q: Explain how standard electrode potentials are measured, how they predict whether a reaction will occur, and predict whether zinc will displace copper from copper sulphate solution.
questions.solution:
**Measuring $E^{\ominus}$.** A potential difference can only be measured between two electrodes, so one is fixed as a reference: the **standard hydrogen electrode**, defined as exactly $0.00$ V.

The half-cell under test is connected to it through a salt bridge, with a high-resistance voltmeter across the two (high resistance so that no current flows and equilibrium is undisturbed).

**Standard conditions:** $298$ K, $100$ kPa, all solutions at $1$ mol dm$^{-3}$.

**Interpreting the values.** A **more negative** $E^{\ominus}$ means the species is more readily **oxidised** — a better reducing agent.

A **more positive** $E^{\ominus}$ means it is more readily **reduced** — a better oxidising agent.

**Predicting a reaction.** The half-cell with the **more positive** $E^{\ominus}$ runs as written (reduction); the other runs in reverse (oxidation).

$E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{more positive}} - E^{\ominus}_{\text{more negative}}$, and a **positive** result means feasible.

**Zinc and copper sulphate.**

$\text{Zn}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \to \text{Zn}$, $E^{\ominus} = -0.76$ V

$\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \to \text{Cu}$, $E^{\ominus} = +0.34$ V

Copper's is more positive, so copper is reduced and zinc is oxidised:

$\text{Zn} + \text{Cu}^{2+} \to \text{Zn}^{2+} + \text{Cu}$, with $E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = +1.10$ V

**Feasible** — and this is what is seen: the blue colour fades and copper deposits on the zinc.

**Two warnings.** $E^{\ominus}$ values assume **standard conditions**; concentrations far from $1$ mol dm$^{-3}$ can reverse a marginal prediction. And feasibility says nothing about **rate** — a reaction with $E^{\ominus} = +2$ V may be immeasurably slow if its activation energy is high.

questions.q: Describe the shape of the pH curve for a strong acid titrated with a strong base, and compare it with a weak acid titrated with a strong base. Explain how the indicator is chosen.
questions.solution:
**Strong acid with strong base.**

The curve starts at about pH 1 and rises very slowly at first, since the acid is in large excess.

Near the equivalence point it becomes almost **vertical**, sweeping from about pH 3 to pH 11 on the addition of a fraction of a drop.

The **equivalence point is at pH 7**, because the salt formed is neutral.

**Weak acid with strong base.**

It starts higher, at about pH 3 — the weak acid gives fewer hydrogen ions.

There is then a **buffer region**, where the curve rises only gently: the mixture of unreacted acid and the salt being formed is itself a buffer. At the half-equivalence point, $\text{pH} = \text{p}K_{a}$ — a convenient way of measuring $K_{a}$.

The vertical section is **shorter**, roughly pH 7 to 11, and the **equivalence point is above 7** (about 8.7), because the salt of a weak acid hydrolyses to give an alkaline solution.

**Choosing the indicator.** An indicator must change colour **entirely within the vertical section**, so that the change is sharp and occurs at the equivalence point.

• **Strong-strong:** the vertical range is huge, so either **phenolphthalein** ($8.3$–$10$) or **methyl orange** ($3.1$–$4.4$) works.

• **Weak acid with strong base:** only **phenolphthalein** — methyl orange would change far too early, while acid remained.

• **Strong acid with weak base:** only **methyl orange**.

• **Weak acid with weak base:** there is **no vertical section at all**, so no indicator is suitable, and a pH meter must be used.

**Note that the indicator does not need to change at pH 7** — it needs to change where the curve is vertical, which is a different requirement and the one that matters.

questions.q: State Faraday's laws of electrolysis and calculate the mass of copper deposited by a current of $2$ A flowing for $30$ minutes through copper(II) sulphate solution. ($A_{r}(\text{Cu}) = 63.5$, $F = 96\,500$ C/mol.)
questions.solution:
**First law.** The mass deposited is proportional to the quantity of electricity passed: $m \propto Q = It$.

**Second law.** The same quantity of electricity deposits amounts of different substances in the ratio of their **equivalent masses** — the molar mass divided by the number of electrons involved.

**The calculation.**

$Q = It = 2 \times 1800 = 3600$ C

$\text{moles of electrons} = \dfrac{3600}{96\,500} = 0.0373$ mol

$\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \to \text{Cu}$, so **two** electrons per copper atom:

$\text{moles of Cu} = \dfrac{0.0373}{2} = 0.01865$ mol

$\text{mass} = 0.01865 \times 63.5 = \mathbf{1.18}$ g

**The step most often missed** is dividing by the charge on the ion. For silver ($\text{Ag}^{+}$) there is no division; for aluminium ($\text{Al}^{3+}$) the division is by three.

**Where this is used industrially.** Electroplating, purifying copper (the impure metal is the anode, pure copper the cathode, and the precious-metal impurities collect below as anode sludge worth recovering), and extracting aluminium — which consumes about $5\%$ of the electricity generated in some countries.

**And the reverse process** is a battery, where the same electrode reactions run spontaneously and deliver current rather than consuming it.
